utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon. Assisting me today will be, to my right, Mr. Fergal Gaynor, and to his right, Mr. Ulrich Mussemeyer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Dan Brashich for the Krajisnik defence, and I'm joined by Goran Neskovic of the Republika Srpska bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Robert Pavich on behalf of the defendant Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a hearing in order to deal, first of all, with the Status Conference at some stage, probably later; first of all, to consider three motions and hear oral argument upon them insofar as oral argument is necessary. The three motions are a motion on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik to compel the disclosure of exculpatory evidence under Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; secondly, a Prosecution motion for clarification in respect of Rule 65 ter, 66, and 67; and thirdly, a motion on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik to compel the Prosecution to provide the identity of subordinates. Can I say at the outset that there have been oral submissions in relation to all three of these motions. The Prosecution has had -- the Court, rather, has had the opportunity of reading those, and there is no need for them to be repeated, so I hope that any oral submissions can be brief. The first issue, then, is the issue of exculpatory evidence. We have Mr. Brashich, your motion. Effectively, you are asking the Prosecution be required to disclose, to identify the exculpatory material rather than merely, as they appear to have done here, to have served you with some many thousand documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. The only thing which I would like to add to my written submission is, one of the reasons why we seek the exculpatory material is that I have not as yet been able to define or divine the Prosecution's case. I am mindful of the position taken by the Court with regard to certain earlier motions. However, under the fair reading of the language of Rule 68, the Prosecution is to "disclose." I read the word "disclose" as an affirmative showing rather than a delivery of the thousands of pages of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you deal with this, Mr. Brashich: One of the things they say is that you've had the documentation and you've had the chance to review it, and therefore their argument is that it would be redundant for them to have to go through this material to determine what's exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: If we had gone through all of the documentation to date, perhaps there might be some validity to the argument. However, my team has only been able to plow through, the last time I was in Bosnia, I believe it was -- I will not like to misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if memory serves me correct, we have been able to go through 14 of the 25 or 26 CDs because it's a labourious task. We do not as yet have the computer ability to go through the remaining disks, so we have to go document through document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, you're not reducing it, as I understand, to a mere question of burden and labour. You're arguing that as a matter of principle, the Prosecution has an obligation under 68 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to make this disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As a matter of principle and as a fair reading of the Rule, they have the obligation to tell me what they consider as to the exculpatory. The reason why I was raising the issue of volume was in response to Judge May's question. But I still stand by my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your first point, of course, that you have not been able to define the Prosecution position --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I think I used both "define" and "divine."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or divine the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, the way the Rules are constructed, the essence of that will come with the pre-trial brief when they are required to set out their case, so that the Defence and also the Court understand it. At this stage, you simply have the indictment and the various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavich, you haven't submitted anything. Do you want to submit something on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, to put this in the context of a decision that Judge Hunt has rendered in a parallel case, to which we were directed at one of our earlier Status Conferences, and in that case, Judge Hunt -- and I'm quoting now from paragraph 19, and it seems to me that this is the context that is helpful for us, within which to consider this. Judge Hunt states: "In a case based upon superior responsibility, what is most material is the relationship between the accused and the others who did acts for which he is alleged to be responsible, and the conduct of the accused by which he may be found to have known or had reason to know that the acts were about to be done or had been done by those others and to have failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm reading text and I'm reading obviously a little too quickly, but to continue: "-- to take reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the persons who did them. However" -- And I think this is the important element that Judge Hunt raises that I believe is relevant here: "However, so far as those acts of the other persons are concerned, although the Prosecution remains under an obligation to give all the particulars which it is able to give, the relevant facts will usually be stated with less precision, and that is because the detail of those acts, by whom and against whom they are done, is often unknown and because the acts themselves cannot be greatly in issue." Your Honour, I believe that Judge Hunt is suggesting to us that the Prosecution should disclose to us all the information that it in fact has. It can't do more than that but the suggestion is that it should do no less. And if the Prosecution does have the identities of these individuals, those identities should be disclosed to enable us to focus upon the real issues that are before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a later motion, isn't it? You're dealing with a later motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: I believe we are dealing with a later motion, but I believe that the thrust of what we are trying to do here, and what the Court has been encouraging us to do, is to try to do sooner what other cases have done later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have filed a pleading in this case. I won't repeat what's in that pleading, but I would like to emphasise some facts. The first fact is that what the Defence is asking us to do is to retroactively go back through these materials and identify for them material that may fall within the ambit of Rule 68. Now, disclosure in this case, Your Honours, has been ongoing. It started on the 7th of April, 2000. It has been a steady production. On the 16th of April, we submitted to the Defence 80.000 to 85.000 pages of material. On the 25th of January 2001, at the Status Conference, the Defence informed the Court that, and I quote, "I have reviewed all the documents that I have received from the Prosecution." Furthermore, the Rules require -- the new Rules require, under pre-trial proceedings, the Defence ultimately identify in general terms the nature of their Defence. We have attempted on numerous occasions to have the defence identified in this case so we can expedite our Rule 68 production, we can focus more precisely on matters that may fall within and surely fall within Rule 68. Currently, we are asked to speculate as to what is possibly Rule 68 material. In essence, Your Honours, the Defence has had this material for a considerable period of time. They've reviewed the majority. Either counsel, the accused, or previous counsel, have reviewed this material that has been produced to the Defence. To ask us now to go back and retroactively attempt to identify for them what may or may not be Rule 68 is, from our point of view at this time, a needless waste of resources. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Our resources have to be devoted to preparing for the trial, not doing work that, in part, has already been done by the Defence. The Defence knows the defence that it intends to raise. It knows the types of documents that are exculpatory under the circumstances. They've seen the indictment, and they are in the best position possible to identify what materials are Rule 68. So those are facts that I'd like to raise with this Trial Chamber and which I believe have a direct bearing on the issue of whether we should be compelled to go back in time and review this quantity of materials for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you say that so far the Defence have not discharged their obligation under the new Rules to identify the general nature of their defence, and that has hampered you, of course, in discharging your obligation under 68. If the Defence were to identify the general nature of their defence, you would then be in a better position to identify exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. Now, under the new Rules, the Defence isn't obligated to identify the general nature of its Defence until it files its defence, its pre-trial brief, but we have invited the Defence on two occasions to identify the general nature of their defence, given the fact that ultimately before trial, they're going to have to do so. We did that with the purpose in mind to quickly and efficiently identify what may fall within the ambit of Rule 68 so we could produce it to the Defence and they could have it at their disposal many, many, many months before the trial is due to commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the other hand, they have suggested that they don't know your case fully, your full case yet, so it is difficult for them to identify exculpatory material. This is a circular argument that we are getting involved in, but we'll have to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next motion is the Prosecution motion which I can shortly refer to as one of reciprocal disclosure, the position being this, that the Prosecution has identified 800 core documents, as they call them, which I take to be documents which they will be relying on at trial. Of those, nearly 400, nearly a half, have been disclosed, but at the last Status Conference, I, as the pre-trial Judge, stated the sooner the documents are disclosed the better and suggested it be done within a month. The Prosecution are now seeking to clarify their position relying on Rule 66(b) and also the reciprocal Rule of 67. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we find ourselves in this position and we seek clarification. At a Status Conference there was a suggestion, and we believe not an order, to provide to the Defence core documents. At the 65 ter conference, I made a request to clarify whether or not we had been ordered to turn over documents. Now, the Defence in its pleading contends that we had been ordered to turn over those core documents, and before I get into my argument, I'd like to correct the record because the 65 ter meeting that was held on the 1st of July, 2001, that very issue was raised, and we were informed that there was no standing order to produce these documents. That is referred to at page 35 of the transcript of the Rule 65 ter meeting. So we operate now on the understanding that there is no such order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Had there been an order, it would have been formulated in those terms; and if that's not clear, what was being suggested was that this proposal be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's any doubt about it and it's thought to be an order, the Trial Chamber does have power in exceptional circumstances to reconsider, of course, any order made by a pre-trial judge. So we are prepared to entertain this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But I wanted to correct the record because in the Defence pleading, Your Honour, they have indicated that there is such an order, and it is quite to the opposite. Now, this is the situation we find ourselves in: We, the Prosecutor's Office, are fully prepared to make disclosure of all of the documents that we intend to use at trial. We're prepared to do so under the Rules that have guided us for many years. We are not prepared to do so on a voluntary basis where there is no quid pro quo. What does that mean? That means that in the case of Mrs. Plavsic, who has invoked reciprocal discovery, we are prepared to provide all of the documents that we're required to under reciprocal discovery provisions, and indeed, we've already started to provide to the Defence some of those additional -- what are characterised here as core documents. I think we have provided an additional 85 documents to the defendant Plavsic. We're prepared to provide all of those documents to the Trial Chamber for its guidance and use and study prior to the commencement of the trial. We are not prepared to provide those documents to defendant Krajisnik who expressly has refused to invoke the provisions of reciprocal discovery. Now, why aren't we prepared to do so? Well, we believe that the Rules themselves have been created with a purpose, and the purpose of those Rules is to create a balance: to give the parties an opportunity to examine the evidence that is going to be introduced in this trial; to have an opportunity to examine whether or not its authentic, whether it's genuine, whether it can be challenged in some way. And what we simply do not want to find ourselves in is in the position where we have given documents to the defendant Krajisnik months, literally months in advance of a tentative trial date, and then find ourselves in a position of receiving documents introduced at trial by the Krajisnik defence the day of trial and having absolutely no opportunity to examine those documents, to study those documents, to attempt to authenticate those documents. There would be a grotesque imbalance under those circumstances, were we to find ourselves in a position that I've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's further down the line. At the moment, we have to deal with your disclosure position. And the present position is this: That you have provided half the core documents - or your predecessor provided half, and you are taking the position that you don't have to provide the other half. What do you say your obligation is under 65 ter at the pre-trial brief stage? Are you prepared to disclose more than a mere list of the exhibits but to disclose the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that raises a separate question and an interesting question. Certainly to the Plavsic Defence, the issue is moot. Were Mrs. Plavsic standing alone in this case, and having revoked reciprocal discovery, I could provide a very detailed list or less than a detailed list, because the Defence would know precisely what documents I intend to use. The question is: In the case of a defendant who refuses to invoke reciprocal discovery, can Rule 65 ter and the description that needs to be furnished of documents that have to be identified in the pre-trial brief circumvent the more explicit disclosure requirements that are found in section 4? And under section 4 -- section 4 of the Rules deals with the disclosure of evidence, and that's where we find, under section 4, Rule 66(B) and Rule 67(C). So it seems to me, in reading the Rules in their entirety, Rule 65 ter is procedural, Rule 66(B) and 67(C) are substantive. They deal with disclosure of information and evidence to the accused. I don't believe, and it's our position and our submission, Your Honours, that the procedural Rules -- the procedural Rule in 65 ter, the identity of evidence, supersedes the reciprocal discovery provisions of Rules 66 and 67. Otherwise, Rule 65 ter makes the reciprocal discovery provisions academic, makes them moot. And that's not what is intended by the Rules of reciprocal discovery. So my answer, then, in the case of a defendant who does not wish to provide the -- submit a request for reciprocal discovery, there is a slightly different answer. And that answer is that the description can be less than a full and complete description. It can be a general description. It can be a summary. But it should do -- in no circumstance should it be permitted to eviscerate the purpose and the intent of the reciprocal discovery provisions that are found in section 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are saying 65 ter must be read subject to 66 and 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you prepared to disclose under 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would be prepared to disclose a more general description of documents. Certainly if they are documents that relate to publications in the Official Gazettes, for example, I can identify those with specificity. But then, when I start to deal with issues of intercepted communications, when I start to deal with issues of specific orders, then I don't believe, and it's our submission, that I'm not required under Rule 65 ter (E)(3), to identify the exhibits with such specificity that it obviates any need or request or any desire to seek reciprocal discovery. This provision in 65 ter isn't designed for discovery purposes, to give the Defence a complete and full opportunity to identify the documents. The appropriate Rules for that is Rule 66(B) and Rule 67(C). Those are the provisions that say if you want to see the documents that we are going to tender in trial, you invoke the provision and you will be permitted to inspect those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How, then, is the Defence to prepare for trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Defence can prepare very easily for trial, the same way Mrs. Plavsic is going to prepare for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But supposing the Defence says, "We don't propose to follow this route. We wish to prepare our Defence on the basis that we are not going to give the Prosecution the right to go through our documents." Supposing that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well then, my answer to you, Your Honour, would be as follows: The Defence is capable of using other tools available at their disposal to prepare for the Defence. They have an indictment that puts them on notice, they have investigators or the ability to travel in the Republika Srpska and elsewhere to acquire the evidence that they need for their Defence. They have available for them binding orders. They can make applications to this Court and seek specific documents from the possessors of those documents, such as the Republika Srpska or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They can prepare their Defence the same way many other defendants have done, absent their request for reciprocal discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But they don't know what they have got to defend because they don't know what these documents are. I'm taking it a bit further down the line. I mean, would you propose during the course of the trial to produce your exhibits and put them before the Court for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, I said earlier that I'm prepared to give the Trial Chamber a list of the exhibits and copies of the exhibits to study well in advance of the commencement of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But would it be right for the Trial Chamber to have them when the defence don't? I foresee many problems. For instance, if this practice were followed, it would delay the trial. It would be up to the Defence to say, "It's the first time we have seen this document. It's immensely damaging and immensely prejudicial, and we need time to prepare. We need time to take instructions."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By the same token, Judge May, that argument applies to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we are submitted -- if we are presented documents that we need to examine and analyse and attempt to authenticate, we also would be asking for a delay. That's why I think the burden of requesting reciprocal discovery -- and reciprocal discovery helps all of us in this courtroom in identifying what are the proper documents, what are the documents that are going to be contested, what are the documents that are at issue in this case? It gives both sides an ample opportunity to prepare. Right now, the Plavsic Defence has asked for reciprocal discovery. Trial has been tentatively scheduled in January, approximately six or seven months from now. The Defence will have ample opportunity, the Plavsic Defence, to analyse these documents. Now, if the co-defendant in this case doesn't wish to avail himself to that procedural set of Rules - and this set of Rules that invite him, that permit him to inspect our documents - then he does so with the full knowledge that he's not going to have the opportunity to examine them in the same amount of time as his co-defendant. But that's his choice. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've done some research on this. The preponderance of practice has been for the Prosecution to produce its documents. There's a difference in practice, clearly, between what's happened in two of the Trial Chambers and what's happened in the third. In the cases before this Trial Chamber, the documents have always been produced without argument, the exhibits, and likewise in the cases before Trial Chamber II. Trial Chamber I, a rather different practice has prevailed. So we are faced with balancing that and considering the effects of the Rules, and also doing justice to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm guided by the Rules. These Rules have been amended, I think, 15 or 20 times, and these Rules have a very clear structure to them, providing an equal opportunity to examine each other's documents if a request is made. There's no Rule that I can see other than Rule 54, which is a general rule that says the Trial Chamber can make any order appropriate for the conduct of the trial, that is applicable. Now, I concede that the Trial Chamber can under Rule 54 make such an order, but it's our submission further that the more explicit Rules under Rule 66(B) and Rule 67(C) have greater weight and have to be considered in considering the totality of the Rules. Rules 66(B) and Rules 67(C) weren't created as decoration or as rules that could be or should be ignored. In the overall scheme of discovery, they were created with a purpose. What we have here is one defendant who simply refuses to request reciprocal discovery and wants Your Honours to impose an order on the Prosecutor that vitiates Rule 66(B) and Rule 67(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be what was intended, it may be that it's not been very felicitously expressed, it may be what is intended by that Rule is for the other party to be able to go through all your documentation. I forget, you have 3 million, sometimes that word is used -- that figure is used. You have a very large amount of documents, many of which, we are pleased to see, that you are not going to use. Now, it may be that what was in the minds of those drafting the Rules, although they haven't expressed it that way, was that if a party wanted to go through all of your documentation, then that would trigger reciprocal discovery. But you say that Rule 54 which, as you concede, is a Rule that we could use, but that we cannot or should not use it to override what you say are the discovery provisions. That's your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And an additional point needs to be clarified and that is the number of 3 million documents. I think it needs to be perfectly clear, in the Defence submission they say 3 million documents apply to documents that we have acquired from the Republika Srpska. That's not correct. The figure, first of all, I am informed, is approximately 2.7 million, not that it makes a big difference; but second of all, those documents relate to documents that are in our entire database that apply to the Bosnian Croats, Croatia, Republika Srpska, in all of the parties and all of the regions that are within our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a figure that relates to all your documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To all of our documentation, and contrary to the characterisation in the Defence submission, not solely to Republika Srpska documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, unless there's anything else to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position that the Krajisnik defence has taken is not that it refuses to invoke the reciprocal discovery, it chooses not to invoke it. The gross imbalance of which the Prosecution speaks of is somewhat, really, imbalance vis-a-vis the defendant. In the jurisdiction where I come from, the Prosecution does the investigation and then indicts, and shortly thereafter the core documents are made available to the Defence. In this case, we have an indictment which is over a year old, a defendant who has been sitting in gaol for over a year, and discovery is not yet complete, and it is in this context that the Prosecution now wishes to withhold the core documents. I had read Your Honour's suggestion, if it be that, as an order. If it was not an order, I would then move orally for such an order. This is not a civil trial where the -- each party bears a responsibility to either defend and only prove the case by a fair preponderance of the evidence. This is a criminal Prosecution, and the burden falls upon the Prosecution to make available all of its evidence to the Defence. The Defence does not have that particular burden. The Prosecution here is not in a game, who's going to win or lose. The Prosecution is the conscience of the International Community. It has a higher standard than a mere litigant, and if the suggestion made by Your Honour was a mere suggestion, I move orally that that suggestion be made into an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pavich.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of -- Your Honours, just a couple of points, since I'm not directly involved in the conflict that's currently before the Court. First, I do think that the fact that we may have invoked Rule 66(B) and a request to inspect should not deter the Court from confronting the issue because this issue, I believe, will appear again in other cases that will be forthcoming, and I think it would be very helpful if all the parties could get clarification regarding this issue. Secondly, as the Court has also indicated, a possible reason for invoking a Rule 66 request to inspect, as we've done on behalf of Ms. Plavsic, is to have an opportunity to inspect the entire archives of the Prosecutor's Office, and we are discussing that now with the Prosecutor's Office in terms of whether we might be able to get an index of those documents as a starting point to determine which of those 2.7 million documents may be relevant to this case. And I would also suggest that the fact that those documents may extend beyond the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not necessarily indicate that they would not be relevant. In a case of this magnitude, it's quite possible that documents coming from other republics of the former Yugoslavia may be relevant. So I would certainly not disagree with the Court's observation that one of the purposes of a request to inspect documents under Rule 66(B) may be precisely to enable the Defence to have an opportunity to determine what is in the archives, and that is, in fact, one of the reasons that we've made such a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with the third motion which is the motion on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik to compel the Prosecution to provide the identity of subordinates. Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the outset, I don't know whether my motion made on Saturday was accepted to reply on the record to the Prosecution's answer which I received on July 6th. Perhaps that issue is moot since I could very easily address it orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I wish to stress that I'm mindful of the Court's earlier order with regard to bills of particular. I join Mr. Pavich's request that the Court take into consideration Judge Hunt's order of June 26 in the Brdjanin and Talic case, and I would also urge the Court to look at the February 20th decision in that matter which preceded it. A bill of particulars in this case has not been granted, and it has been suggested by the Trial Chamber that the pre-trial order will take its place. As I had suggested in my motion, the Defence is faced with the following: We have 7.1 and 7.3 responsibility, command responsibility. In paragraph 18.2 of the consolidated amendment, there is a charge that at Sikrina [phoen] On May 5 or 7, 1992, 17 Bosnian Muslims and Croats were killed on the territory of Bosanski Samac. The only reason why I know what had occurred on May 7th or 9th, 1992, was because I was lead counsel in the Bosanski Samac case. The individual who allegedly perpetrated this particular crime, these killings, was a man by the name of Lugar, and his last name escapes me. Now, he was a paramilitary who had come to the territory of Bosanski Samac around April 3rd or 5th. At that particular time, there was a Colonel Nikolic who was the military commander. I am being charged under, perhaps 7.1 - I don't know - did my client give a direct order, or under 7.3, superior command. I can't start following up the chain of command from Lugar to my client unless I know the individuals over whom I had command control of. We go Lugar, paramilitary. We can go to Nikolic, colonel of the JNA. If we go to Nikolic JNA on May 7th, there wasn't an Army of the Republika Srpska. Nikolic goes straight to Belgrade, not to my client. If on the other hand, it is the Prosecution theory that Lugar, last name unknown, is under the direct control of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac, then I have got to go to Blagoje Simic in Scheveningen and say, "Did you Blagoje Simic have a direct command control with my client in Pale?" So unless I get the identity of these individuals, I can't send out my investigators, I can't start, and I could not even argue the reasonableness of my request. As an example with Bosanski Samac, I just don't know, but I have given you a concrete example of why the Prosecution should give me this information now. If I get it at a later date, if I get it during the middle of trial - all of a sudden I find out that Lugar is the person who allegedly had perpetrated these killings - then I've got to go and find Lugar. Well, Lugar is dead. So now I have to go to secondary evidence and I cannot adequately prepare Mr. Krajisnik's Defence without that information. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution's arguments in relation to this motion have been set out in our motion of the 6th of July, and I won't bring you through those arguments in detail. The Prosecution today, and indeed in his motions, appears to accept to what he is essentially attacking is the form of the indictment. He is essentially claiming that the indictment is insufficiently particular in relation to the identity of subordinates, aiders and abbettors. As you're well aware, this is essentially the Prosecution's third bite of this particular apple. This Trial Chamber ruled on the 1st of August 2000 that: "There is no lack of precision in the pleading of the material facts in the indictment, as the facts are sufficiently pleaded, and it would be unreasonable to ask the Prosecution for further precision." Trial Chamber went on to say: "Having regard to the higher level of responsibility alleged against this accused, the Trial Chamber finds that the Prosecution has satisfied, for the purpose of the indictment, the requirements for specificity in setting out, among other things, the persons who committed the alleged crimes." What the Defence for Mr. Krajisnik today are essentially asking is for this Trial Chamber to revisit that decision and to revisit the decision of the 8th of May 2001, at which this Trial Chamber, for the second time, rejected the Defence's application for particulars. The Defence have failed in their motion of the 25th of June, and in the motion which we received last night, to provide any reasons on which this Trial Chamber should reverse its earlier two decisions. Today, we hear arguments in relation to a person called Mr. Lugar. Prosecution's position on this is that the Defence is confusing facts which are pleaded in an indictment and evidence which is required to prove those facts. The distinction was made very clear by Your Honours in your decision of the 1st of August 2000 where you said: "There is a difference between the facts of the case and the evidence required to prove those facts. The facts must be pleaded while the evidence is adduced at trial. It follows that disputes as to issues of fact are for determination at trial and not via motions relating to the form of the indictment." Your Honours, in relation to notice, the Defence not only has the indictment and the confirming materials which were handed over in May of 2000, they also have 350 witness statements, 393 core documents, and on the 31st of August, they shall receive the pre-trial brief. As we are all aware, the pre-trial brief must contain a summary of the evidence which the Prosecutor intends to bring regarding the commission of the alleged crime and the form of responsibility incurred by the accused. Prosecution's position is that, as this Trial Chamber has already twice held that the indictment has been pleaded to the requisite degree of specificity, it would be entirely inappropriate for the Defence to be granted the relief which it now seeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Brashich, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I do not seek facts. I seek names. And I don't see what the problem is as giving up the names now. I then have half of July and all of August to send my investigators out. I just don't understand why it is like pulling teeth to get information from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider these motions and will give our decisions in due course in writing. We will go on to consider procedural matters and the status of the proceedings. The Chamber notes that there have been meetings with the Senior Legal Officer, and we would encourage the continuance of those, in order to move things further along. I will ask Mr. Harmon if there is anything the Prosecution want to raise. I believe there are some problems about redaction, which are going to need attention, and also the Rule 92 bis statements, and perhaps you could help us, if you can, with the status of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the 22nd of June, the Krajisnik Defence withdrew its consent to a previous agreement that it would receive redacted statements at least 21 days prior to the trial testimony -- prior to the trial or the testimony. Now, we accept that alteration of a previous agreement, and we have been attempting to contact certain -- all of those witnesses who had previously been protected in that measure, and we continue to do so. We will provide approximately 150 unredacted statements to the Defence, and we are in the process, and should be complete in the process, of turning over to the Defence by the 31st of August all of the witness statements in unredacted form, absent request, special request, for protective measures which may inevitably appear as we continue in this ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you propose to hand over unredacted statements unless there is an application for protective measures in relation to a particular witness which you will have to make to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, provided that's done in good time, there can be no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the 92 bis issue is a different issue, and one that we are also addressing. 92 bis is a recent enactment, a change to the Rules - I think it was published in mid-January of this year - and as Your Honours are aware, the compliance with the Rule itself, in other words getting the declaration, requires enormous logistical -- imposes enormous logistical burdens on us. Now, we are in a position now to turn over approximately 18 statements, where there have been declarations prepared under Rule 92 bis. We are in the process of identifying 92 bis witnesses, and I believe we have identified approximately 186 witnesses who we believe we would be submitting statements under that Rule. We are awaiting a decision of a motion that we filed, I believe, on the 7th of May, requesting that the Registrar appoint a presiding officer pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and we don't have a decision on that. The question becomes this, as far as the office of Prosecutor is concerned: Under the Rules, under the Rule 65 ter - let me find the subpart - 65 ter (E)(ii)(e), we have to, first of all, provide the names of all of the witnesses in our pre-trial brief, and under small (e), we have to indicate whether those witnesses are going to testify in person or pursuant to 92 bis by way of a written statement or use of a transcript of testimony. We are prepared to make that indication in a timely fashion. We can do that by the 31st of August, or come very, very close to 100 per cent compliance with that subpart of the rule. Where the rule becomes more problematic for us is Rule 66(A)(ii), because under the rules, under that particular rule, we have to provide to the Defence "copies of all written statements taken in accordance with Rule 92 bis." Now, we will be providing to the Defence by the 31st of August the witness statements of August of our witnesses. We will provide them in our trial brief with the indications of which of those witnesses will be testifying, or which of those witnesses will be indicated as 92 bis witnesses. But whether we will be able to fully complete the requirements of 92 bis, in other words, acquire the declaration from each of those witnesses who have been identified as such, is a problem for us. And it is one that we are addressing, but I'm not particularly optimistic that by the 31st of August we will have completed all of that process, particularly since we're still awaiting for a decision from an application that we have made, and because it imposes, as I say, large, enormous logistical burdens to fully comply with that. Now, it seems to me that the Defence will be fully notified as to which witnesses are going to be called under Rule 92 bis by us, they will have their complete statement, and so they will not be at any disadvantage if procedurally under Rule 92 bis we haven't finally obtained by the 31st of August the declaration and fully complied with the procedures, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I would have thought that if you were doing as much as you can in regard to that, you will have complied with the Rule as far as you can, provided there's disclosure of the statements and an indication whether the witness is going to be a Rule 92 bis witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We intend to do that, Judge May. It's just a question of whether this Rule under 66(A)(ii) require that we complete in toto the process described in Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you need further time to do it, you can ask for it, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that particular point, I would like some guidance from the Chamber. Does the service of the pre-trial brief kick in the provisions of a 92 bis (E), the 14-day Rule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider it and give you -- we'll give you adequate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I notice the way it's worded that it simply says, "... seeking to adduce a written statement, shall give 14 days' notice." It doesn't say that the statement has to be produced, although I rather think that was what was intended. It would be on receipt of the statement that the 14 days would start to run, but we'll have to think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, anything anybody else would like to raise? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would be raising and filing with the Court in due course an application to expand the length of the pre-trial brief. Given the mathematics that I've done in this case, the number of witnesses and the requirements of the Rule which require us to summarise the testimony of approximately 400 witnesses, it's hard for me to imagine that we can do that in 50 pages. So we will be making application shortly with a proposal, as well, to expand the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Now, as far as the Defence are concerned, are there any matters that anyone wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Motion Hearing adjourned at
